Version 2.0

Access, Compliance, Removals and Enforcement General Instructions

About this guidance

This guidance provides information for Immigration Enforcement officers (“you”) on how to conduct an illegal working operation. It does not replace the legislation, civil penalty regulations, or code of practice, and should be read together with relevant sections and articles mentioned within.

Contacts

If you have read the relevant legislation, this guide and the Employer’s guide to right to work checks and still require more help with an illegal working operation, you must ask your line manager for assistance in the first instance.

If the question cannot be answered at line manager level, you may email (as appropriate):

Civil Penalty Compliance Team (CPCT) communication and correspondence

Right to Work Policy Team

Criminal and Financial Investigations

Enforcement Policy

The Work Casework Risk Team

You can signpost employers who have general enquiries about illegal working and right to work checks to the Home Office Employer Enquiry helpline on 0300 790 6268.

If you notice any formatting errors in this guidance (broken links, spelling mistakes and so on) or have any comments about the layout or navigability of the guidance then you can contact the Guidance Rules and Forms Team.

The full list of documents and tools that support employers are:

Employer’s guide to right to work checks

Right to Work Checklist

Code of practice on preventing illegal working: Right to Work Scheme for employers

Avoiding discrimination while preventing illegal working: code of practice

Illegal working civil penalties: an employer’s guide

an online interactive tool Checking a job applicant’s right to work

an online interactive tool Employer Checking Service

Publication

Below is information on when this version of the guidance was published:

version 2.0

published for Home Office staff on 26 October 2026

Changes from the last version of this guidance

updated guidance to reflect changes introduced by Section 48 of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025, including the extension of the Right to Work Scheme (“the Scheme”) and associated civil penalty liability from 1 October 2026 to a wider range of working arrangements - this includes individuals engaged under a worker’s contract, individual sub-contractors, and certain online matching services

updated definitions throughout the guidance, including the definitions of ‘illegal worker’, ‘working illegally’, and organisations or persons who may be liable for a civil penalty under the Scheme, to align with current legislation and policy

updated references to the latest Employer’s guide to right to work checks and Code of Practice on preventing illegal working

updated criminal offence and civil penalty references to reflect current legislation, including the offence of knowingly employing, or having reasonable cause to believe, that an individual is disqualified from working

updated sponsorship guidance to reflect current sponsor compliance processes and referral arrangements

removed superseded material, including guidance on Croatian national employment restrictions, and consolidated related material on evidence gathering, criminal action, statutory excuses, and supporting employers.

reviewed and updated contact details, cross-references and links to related guidance, legislation, and operational products

general updates to terminology, formatting and drafting to improve consistency with current Home Office guidance standards, including replacing references to ’employees’ with ’workers’, where appropriate

Legislation

You must be familiar with the following legislation when conducting illegal working operations:

Sections 14A to 25 – Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006

The Immigration (Restrictions on Employment) Order 2007

Section 24B - Immigration Act 1971

The legislation listed above provides the core legal framework for the prevention of illegal working in the UK, including right to work checks, the working arrangements within scope of the Scheme, and the civil and criminal sanctions that may apply.

Legislation What it covers

Sections 14A to 25 of the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006. The Right to Work Scheme, including civil penalty liability under the Scheme and the criminal offence relating to employing an individual who is disqualified from working by reason of their immigration status.

The Immigration (Restrictions on Employment) Order 2007. The requirements relating to right to work checks and establishing a statutory excuse against civil penalty liability.

Section 24B of the Immigration Act 1971. The criminal offence of illegal working.

When the Right to Work Scheme applies

The Scheme has applied to employment (under a contract of service or apprenticeship) commencing on or after 29 February 2008.

From 1 October 2026, the scheme also applies to a wider range of working arrangements, including where an organisation either:

engages an individual under a worker’s contract

engages an individual sub-contractor

operates an online matching service that provides details of individual service providers to potential clients or customers

In some circumstances, civil penalty liability may also extend beyond the employer who has the direct contractual relationship with the worker. Further guidance on extended liability is provided below.

The changes introduced from 1 October 2026 are not retrospective. This means they do not create liability under new provisions in relation to working arrangements entered into before that date.

You must consider the potential nature of the working arrangement to guide your questioning and gather evidence about how it operates and when it commenced. The Civil Penalty Compliance Team (CPCT) will consider the evidence and determine the type of working arrangement and the provisions that apply.

Potential extended liability

Where potential extended liability is identified during a visit, you must issue a NOPL to each potentially liable employer or person present at the premises. This may require more than 1 NOPL to be issued.

You are not required to determine whether the prescribed contractual requirements have been met or whether the evidence establishes a statutory excuse under the extended liability provisions. You must record and retain all relevant evidence and provide it to CPCT so that it can assess the contractual arrangements and determine liability.

Where another potentially liable person or business is not present, or their commercial or business premises have not been visited, the absence of a NOPL does not prevent the case from being referred to CPCT for consideration.

Any relevant documents provided should be copied and attached to the Pronto record or sent to the CPCT Referrals inbox quoting the enforcement visit reference number.

Completing and issuing the NOPL

The NOPL must include:

the name and role or job title of the individual to whom it is issued

the date it is issued

the relevant enforcement visit reference

the employer or business name and registered address

the business type

VAT and company number, where applicable

the names of any directors or owners

the date and address at which the illegal working was encountered

the names and dates of birth of the relevant illegal workers

the reason for referral for each worker

You must complete 1 NOPL and as many additional worker supplements (AWS) as required to record all relevant illegal workers.

Where a commercial or business premises is visited, the NOPL must be issued at the time of the visit. You must issue the notice even where further enquiries are required. A photograph of the completed NOPL must be uploaded to Pronto.

Where a potential breach of the Scheme is identified away from the employer’s commercial or business premises, for example where a delivery rider is encountered while making a delivery, there is no requirement to subsequently serve a NOPL on the employer by post. Please note that the absence of a NOPL does not prevent referral to CPCT.

Where the commercial or business premises of a potentially liable employer or person are visited, you must issue a NOPL.

Criminal action

This section explains what you must do when you suspect that a criminal offence has been committed during an illegal working operation.

Suspected criminal offences

If, during exploratory questioning or an administrative interview, you develop reasonable grounds to suspect that a criminal offence may have been committed you must stop questioning about the suspected offence and refer the matter to the appropriate Criminal and Financial Investigations (CFI) team or CFI duty manager as soon as possible.

This may include suspected offences relating to:

employing an illegal worker

illegal working

facilitation

modern slavery, human trafficking, forced labour, or related offences

You must record the referral and follow any advice provided by CFI to ensure that any subsequent arrest, interview, or seizure of evidence is conducted in accordance with the relevant legislation and guidance.

Where CFI advises that an individual should be arrested, you must caution the individual and explain the reason for their arrest. See: Arrest and restraint.

For further information on questioning and interviews, see: Enforcement interviews.

Civil penalty and criminal action

A potential civil penalty and a suspected criminal offence may arise from the same circumstances.

Where you suspect that an employer may be liable for a civil penalty, but do not suspect that the employer has committed a criminal offence, you may continue to gather the information necessary for evidencing a breach of the scheme.

Where you suspect that an employer has also committed a criminal offence, you must stop questioning about the suspected offence and seek advice from CFI.

A worker may commit the offence of illegal working whether or not civil or criminal action is taken against an employer. Where criminal action against the worker may be appropriate, refer the matter to CFI.

CFI will determine whether criminal action is appropriate in accordance with the relevant guidance and circumstances of the case. See also:

Arrest and restraint

Enforcement interviews

Dealing with potential criminality

Identifying people at risk

Supporting employers

This section explains how to respond where an employer asks you for advice about preventing illegal working or reports suspected illegal working.

You must take care when advising employers and ensure that any advice is consistent with published Home Office guidance. You must not advise an employer on individual employment decisions or provide assurances about whether or not civil penalty or criminal action will be taken in cases involving illegal working.

Cooperation by an employer does not prevent civil penalty or criminal action. Relevant mitigating factors will be considered as part of any subsequent civil penalty or criminal investigation process.

General advice about preventing illegal working

Employers seeking general advice about preventing illegal working or help conducting a right to work check should be directed to the relevant employer support services and GOV.UK guidance:

The Home Office Employer Enquiry helpline on 0300 790 6268

Penalties for employing illegal workers which provides access to guidance on preventing illegal working
